item.title: Ethiopia launches polio vaccination campaign to protect more than 11 million children: WHO deployed 28 staff to support the vaccination campaign
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: World Health Organization

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 21 November 2026 – The Government of Ethiopia, in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) partners, and other partners, launched a polio vaccination campaign aimed at protecting more than 11.3 million children from poliovirus infection. The polio vaccination campaign, which is launched today, 21 November 2026 will be implemented across five regions including Addis Ababa, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, South Ethiopia and Southwest Ethiopia. Speaking on the launch of the polio vaccination held today in Arba Minch, South Ethiopia Region, Dr Loveday Nkwogu who delivered the partner’s joint speech on behalf of Prof. Francis Kasolo, WHO Representative to Ethiopia, emphasized the importance of collective action to protect children from polio.

"Every child vaccinated during this vaccination campaign brings Ethiopia to contributing one step closer to a polio-free future. While significant progress has been made, poliovirus continues to threaten children wherever immunity gaps exist. We call on parents, community leaders, health workers and partners to join forces to ensure that every eligible child is reached, protected and given a healthy start in life."

WHO has deployed 28 it’s central and field staff to support this vaccination campaign. WHO’s technical team have been supporting key activities to ensure that all eligible children are reached during the vaccination campaign including coordination, advocacy, microplanning, Training of health workers at national and regional level, training of supervisors for the Open Data Kit (ODK) utilization, as well as for Independent monitors and lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) surveyors to be deployed during and after the vaccination campaign to ensure its quality, to support supervision on the campaign implementation, data management, and community engagement to ensure the quality of the vaccination campaign.

The first round of the vaccination campaign will be conducted from 21-24 November 2026, followed by a second round from 18-21 December 2026. During the vaccination campaign, a vaccination team composed of health workers and community volunteers will conduct a house-to-house visits to vaccinate every eligible child in the household with life-saving polio vaccine to protect against polio.

In addition to administering polio vaccines, the vaccination teams will identify zero-dose and under-vaccinated children during the house-to-house visits and link them with routine immunization services to ensure they receive the missed routine vaccines.

Although Ethiopia remains free of wild poliovirus, outbreaks of circulating variant poliovirus continue to pose a threat, particularly in areas with immunity gaps and high population movement. This year, cases of circulating variant poliovirus type 1 were reported from Gambella, Oromia and South Ethiopia regions, underscoring the need for rapid and high-quality vaccination responses to protect children and stop transmission. Similar polio vaccination campaigns have been already conducted in Gambella and Benishangul Gumuz Region and two Zones of Oromia Region (West Wolleag and Kelm Wollega).

The current polio vaccination campaign builds on the success of previous outbreak response efforts conducted in Gambella, Benishangul-Gumuz and parts of Oromia region, which reached more than 1 million children and demonstrated the effectiveness of coordinated action among government authorities, communities, health workers and partners.

WHO and partners are also calling for increasing efforts to strengthen vaccine preventable surveillance alongside with vaccination efforts. High-quality Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) and environmental surveillance remain essential to rapidly detect and respond to any poliovirus transmission and safeguard the gains achieved in polio eradication efforts.

The World Health Organization continues to provide technical and operational support to the Government of Ethiopia, including during planning, coordination, monitoring, supervision and surveillance activities, as part of the global effort to eradicate polio once and for all.

Ethiopia joins the global community in reaffirming its commitment to ensuring that no child is missed, no community is left behind, and every child is protected from vaccine-preventable diseases.

item.title: Kenya: Gender-based violence: a public health and human rights concern
item.description:
Country: Kenya
Source: World Health Organization

Nairobi— Married at the age of 14, Mparakoni Leabune from Samburu County in northern Kenya was the third wife in a polygamous union. “My husband used to beat me a lot," she says. "That is how I got this leg injury," she says pointing to severe swelling on her left leg. Despite countless medical interventions, Leabune has endured a long and painful road to recovery.
"My husband divorced me and now I live with my mother," she says.

Aside from enduring physical violence, Leabune is a survivor of early marriage, which is also considered a form of gender-based violence.

According to Kenya’s 2022 Demographic Health Survey, more than a third of women (34%) in Kenya have experienced physical violence since the age of 15 years, and 13% have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime. Nine out of 10 times, the perpetrator is a either a current or former husband or partner.

Furthermore, according to the 2025/2026 Kenya Mini-Demographic Heath Survey, technology- facilitated gender-based violence is on the rise: more than a quarter of women aged age 15–49 have ever experienced it from any perpetrator. Technology- facilitated gender-based violence includes acts such as online harassment, cyberbullying and online control to cause harm.
“Women are suffering silently because they cannot seek medical attention, not because of their own will, but because of the patriarchal society we live in," says Samson Esward Leerte, nurse and reproductive health coordinator for adolescents and young people in Samburu County.

The 2010 Constitution protects people in Kenya from harmful cultural practices and violence. Several laws have been enacted and most recently, the National Policy on Gender-based Violence and the National Policy for the Eradication of Female Genital Mutilation were adopted in 2019.

The country is taking steps to ramp up implementation of these laws.

In January 2025, President Williams Ruto established a technical working group on gender-based violence, including femicide. In November 2025, he heard its recommendations. They include several recommendations to curb femicide and female genital mutilation and operationalizing one-stop gender-based violence recovery centres in every county.

In July 2026, the Government of Kenya, through the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action under the Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services and partners convened a national consultative forum on the implementation of the recommendations and sustainability.

"The Ministry of Health remains committed to strengthening the health sector's role in preventing and responding to gender-based violence. Our priority is to ensure that women and girls can access timely, quality and survivor-centred services, while strengthening prevention, early identification, referral and coordination across the health system and with other sectors," says Mary Gathitu, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Programme Lead at Kenya's Ministry of Health. "Ultimately, protecting women and girls from violence requires sustained, coordinated action at both national and county levels."

World Health Organization (WHO) has supported Ministry of Health to conduct assessments of health facility readiness to respond to gender-based violence cases in six counties and has trained more than 250 health workers on the clinical management of gender-based violence survivors since 2025. The Organization also sits on the technical working group that provides support to Ministry of Health on gender-based violence interventions.

“Gender-based violence, particularly intimate partner and sexual violence, is a major public health and human rights concern, rooted in unequal gender norms and power dynamics," says Dr. Rita Arogo, Maternal and Reproductive Health Officer at WHO Kenya. "Its prevention and elimination must be elevated as a priority for action and advocacy at the highest levels."

item.title: Somalia: FLER activation: IDP assessment and community consultations in Afgooye District, Lower Shabelle Region (21 September 2026)
item.description:
Country: Somalia
Sources: Norwegian Refugee Council, SOS Children's Villages International

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive Summary

Between 29 August and 13 September 2026, intensified security operations and armed confrontations in parts of Lower Shabelle, including Basra, Alifow, Baqdaad and Areer Mooge, displaced more than 860 households (approximately 5,100 people, including about 3,640 children) towards Afgooye and surrounding communities, according to cluster/ABC reporting. An estimated 620 children are currently out of school.

SOS Children’s Villages Somalia conducted a field visit and community dialogue in four IDP locations in Lafoole (Waafi, Docol, Durdur and Takulo) to verify the presence of newly displaced families, understand education and protection needs, and identify potential FLER sites. The assessment identified 402 newly displaced households. Education is the most urgent gap: existing public schools are located approximately 1 km to more than 3 km from the settlements, and children who remain out of school face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, family separation, early marriage and psychosocial distress.

Immediate FLER activation is therefore strongly justified. FLER will provide safe, structured learning, psychosocial support, play and life-skills activities, foundational learning and protection identification and referral, while creating a pathway into neighbouring schools. Docol and Durdur IDP Community Centres are the priority FLER locations, covering multiple surrounding IDP subcamps.

item.title: World: Preparedness for the next crisis means planning for the one after it
item.description:
Country: World
Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network

Giuseppe Saba

As the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon in March 2026 intensified humanitarian needs and displacement, the ability to respond quickly depended in part on decisions made before the emergency. By 1 May 2026, UNHCR reported that, together with shelter sector partners, it had delivered relief items to more than 200,000 displaced people, largely using pre-positioned supplies. Additional support included 40 trucks carrying more than 317 metric tonnes of critical aid from Dubai. Preparedness enabled the response.

Stocks, logistics infrastructure and multiple transport options were available before the operating environment deteriorated. This flexibility is increasingly essential in humanitarian logistics. Conflict can escalate while teams are responding to floods elsewhere; a disease outbreak can increase demand as border restrictions constrain supply; and disruption to a single transport route can affect operations far beyond the crisis that caused it. Overlapping emergencies place simultaneous pressure on the same people, supplies, funding and logistics networks.

Preparedness must therefore preserve the capacity to adapt under pressure. That requires strategically positioned supplies, alternative routes and suppliers, visibility of available stocks, established cross-sector relationships, and mechanisms that link early warning to early action. These options need to be in place before a response is under strain.

Prepare for crises that overlap

Other operational lessons from the past six years began with Covid-19. The pandemic showed how quickly disruption in one part of the humanitarian system could propagate across others. Border closures, shifting regulations and competition for transport and essential goods constrained supply chains as demand increased, while humanitarian organisations continued to respond to conflict, displacement, food insecurity and natural hazards.

Subsequent crises have reinforced the same lesson. Emergencies overlap, compete for shared resources, and can disrupt the systems needed to respond to one another. Preparedness therefore needs to account for interacting risks and cumulative demand across the humanitarian system.

Stress-testing should reflect these conditions: a major transport route becoming unavailable during a disease outbreak; stocks allocated to one response being required for another; or several organisations competing for the same aircraft, warehouse or supplier. These scenarios reveal likely capacity constraints and identify where alternatives need to be established in advance.

The practical shift is towards preparing the humanitarian system to operate under cumulative pressure. Organisations need visibility over critical dependencies, the speed at which resources can be redirected, and the decisions required when several responses draw on the same capacity.

Pre-position for flexibility

Pre-positioning reduces response time and preserves operational flexibility as conditions change. Supplies held in strategically connected locations can be deployed rapidly after a sudden-onset emergency and redirected when borders close, transport capacity contracts, or the original response plan becomes unviable.

The February 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye and Syria demonstrated the value of rapid deployment from pre-positioned capacity. Within hours, the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Logistics Centre began mobilising emergency health supplies, and 110 metric tonnes of trauma and surgical supplies were dispatched in the initial response. WHO also drew immediately on supplies already positioned in Syria, showing how stocks at different levels of the supply chain can reinforce one another when response time is critical.

The Lebanon response described at the outset demonstrates a second value: preserving operational options as needs and access conditions evolve. In March 2026, 21.5 metric tonnes of WHO medical supplies were also transported overland from pre-positioned UNCHR stocks in Dubai to Lebanon in four trucks to support healthcare assistance for displaced communities. These movements demonstrate the value of regional connectivity, established partnerships and operational readiness.

Pre-positioning creates optionality. It gives humanitarian organisations a prepared base from which stocks can be released quickly, transport modes adapted, and assistance kept moving as conditions change. Effective preparedness creates the capacity to respond when an emergency unfolds differently from the original plan.

Stock-positioning decisions should therefore weigh historical demand and proximity against connectivity, customs arrangements and alternative onward routes. A well-positioned stockpile enables rapid deployment and preserves viable pathways when the preferred route fails.

Design redundancy across the supply chain

Supply chains concentrated around a single supplier, port, border crossing or transport route can become critical points of failure during a disruption. Humanitarian organisations need to identify these concentrations and establish credible alternatives for the dependencies that pose the greatest operational risk.

Resource constraints make comprehensive duplication unrealistic. Resilience can instead be built by qualifying alternative suppliers in advance, maintaining access to multiple ports or airports, distributing critical stock across locations, and identifying the failures with the greatest operational consequences so that viable alternatives are ready.

Redundancy also has a system-wide dimension. The humanitarian system collectively holds substantial stocks, logistics infrastructure and operational capacity across organisations and hubs. Greater visibility and coordination of that capacity can strengthen resilience without requiring each organisation to replicate the same capabilities.

Preparedness therefore depends on understanding the capacity available across the wider system, the conditions under which it can be accessed, and the speed at which it can be mobilised. This is particularly important during concurrent emergencies, when an organisation’s own stocks or logistics capacity may already be committed elsewhere.

Treat information as preparedness infrastructure

Collective capacity is useful only when decision-makers can see what is available. Humanitarian stocks are held across multiple organisations and locations; governments hold customs and movement information; and logistics providers hold data on transport capacity and constraints. Preparedness needs to turn these separate information sources into a usable operational picture before a crisis creates urgent demand for it.

The Humanitarian Logistics Databank offers one model. The platform brings together information on humanitarian stocks held across the Dubai Humanitarian hub. By combining data on the quantity, location, ownership and movement of relief supplies, including customs data from ports and airports, the platform gives participating organisations a clearer view of available capacity.

This visibility supports faster operational decisions: identifying supplies already positioned near an emerging crisis; determining what needs to be mobilised, rerouted or procured; and understanding what resources may already be available elsewhere in the humanitarian system.

Connecting visibility across hubs makes distributed capacity more actionable: agencies can identify existing resources across locations before establishing new supply chains or moving supplies over longer distances. The value increases when several emergencies draw simultaneously on limited stocks and logistics capacity.

Scaling this model requires more than technical connectivity. Each new hub must align customs regimes, data-sharing rules and operational mandates across governments, agencies and private operators. Extending shared visibility is therefore a policy and governance challenge as well as a technical one, and progress will depend on sustained institutional alignment.

Shared visibility also depends on trust. Participating actors need confidence in data quality, clarity on access and use, and agreed protocols for information sharing. Establishing these arrangements during preparedness enables data to support decisions immediately when a crisis begins.

Build relationships before they are tested

Preparedness is also relational. Governments, United Nations agencies, international and local organisations, customs authorities, donors and private-sector partners each control capabilities or make decisions that can become critical during an emergency.

The Global Health Cluster’s examination of the Covid-19 response highlighted the contributions of civil society, local partners and community leaders, as well as collaboration with government ministries, law enforcement and the private sector. It recommended embedding multisectoral and community-based mechanisms within preparedness so they are operational before a crisis.

The same principle applies across emergency types. Established relationships with government and customs authorities can help organisations respond to changing access conditions; relationships with logistics providers can unlock alternative transport capacity; and national and local organisations can sustain access when international teams cannot reach affected communities.

These relationships require sustained investment in preparedness planning, joint exercises and regular coordination. Local organisations should be involved early, drawing on their knowledge of communities, access constraints and local risks to shape contingency planning, stock positioning and trigger decisions. This embeds localisation within the preparedness architecture from the outset.

Connect early warning to operational readiness

Anticipatory action depends on operational preparedness. Credible forecasts and early warnings can trigger evacuation, cash assistance, protective supplies or measures to protect homes and livelihoods, but the system must already be able to convert warning into action.

That requires linking forecasts to pre-agreed decisions. If severe flooding is predicted, teams should know who can authorise the release of supplies, whether financing is available before a formal emergency declaration, where relevant stocks are held, which partners can reach at-risk communities, and which threshold triggers the response.

Pre-agreed triggers, responsibilities and financing shorten the gap between warning and action. Without them, better forecasting produces earlier awareness, while operational response remains delayed.

Forecasting creates a window for earlier action; preparedness determines whether the system has the resources, authority, partnerships and processes to act.

Putting the lessons into practice

Six years of overlapping crises point to a clear priority: preparedness must be designed for disruption, interaction and change. That means stress-testing for concurrent emergencies, building flexibility into supply chains and pre-positioning, creating visibility of shared capacity, strengthening partnerships in advance, and linking early warning to clear decisions and financing.

Successive and overlapping humanitarian crises have reinforced a clear priority: how much of the response architecture was already in place before the crisis escalated? Stocks, data, routes, partnerships and decision-making mechanisms determine how quickly aid can move and whether it can continue to do so as conditions change.

Humanitarian resilience will depend on the system’s capacity to adapt when events unfold differently from expectations. Embedding that adaptability in planning, coordination and response should be central to preparedness for the crises ahead.

item.title: DR Congo: Casi 6 de cada 10 mujeres y niñas adolescentes encuestadas denuncian un aumento de la violencia y los abusos en Ituri, provincia afectada por el ébola
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: UN Children's Fund

KINSHASA/BUNIA/NUEVA YORK, 24 de noviembre de 2026 – Casi 6 de cada 10 mujeres y niñas adolescentes de 15 años o más encuestadas en Ituri, en la República Democrática del Congo, señalaron la aparición o el aumento de la violencia y los abusos en sus vidas desde que comenzó el brote de ébola.

Los resultados, obtenidos a partir del primer estudio de seguimiento en tiempo real de la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas durante el brote de una enfermedad contagiosa –realizado por UNICEF en colaboración con SOFEPADI, una organización dirigida por mujeres, y la Universidad de Washington en San Luis– revelan la manera en que el brote está afectando a la seguridad de las mujeres y las adolescentes en sus hogares y comunidades.

“Las mujeres y las niñas se enfrentan a una creciente amenaza de violencia y abuso que se suma al brote de una enfermedad mortal y al conflicto que persiste en el este de la República Democrática del Congo”, afirmó Catherine Russell, Directora Ejecutiva de UNICEF. “Con demasiada frecuencia, en las zonas más afectadas no existen espacios de protección fuera del hogar a los que puedan acceder de forma segura”.

Con base en 1.062 entrevistas con mujeres y adolescentes entre el 28 de agosto y el 15 de octubre, los resultados apuntan a la aparición o al aumento de al menos una forma de violencia o abuso. Más de una tercera parte de las encuestadas denunciaron un control cada vez mayor sobre los lugares adonde podían ir, su dinero y sus teléfonos, así como un aumento de los abusos emocionales y psicológicos y de la violencia física y sexual.

Según los hallazgos, 7 de cada 10 encuestadas afirmaron que en su hogar se había aplicado al menos una medida de respuesta en materia de salud pública, como el aislamiento, la cuarentena o el rastreo de contactos. Entre quienes señalaron un aumento de la violencia y los abusos, 9 de cada 10 consideraron que el estrés y el miedo asociados al brote habían contribuido a dicho incremento.

Casi la mitad de las mujeres y las adolescentes que intentaron acceder a servicios de atención y apoyo no pudieron hacerlo. Los trabajadores de primera línea informaron de que algunas mujeres y niñas limitaban sus desplazamientos para evitar contagiarse, mientras que en otros casos eran miembros de la familia u otras personas quienes las obligaban a quedarse encerradas en casa. Algunos de los establecimientos y servicios de los que antes dependían han cerrado o han sido destinados a otros fines. Las encuestadas también citaron la vergüenza, el miedo al agresor y la desconfianza.

La demanda de los espacios seguros que permanecen abiertos y siguen siendo accesibles para las mujeres y las niñas afectadas por la violencia o en riesgo de sufrirla sigue aumentando. Por ejemplo, las visitas a ocho espacios seguros gestionados por SOFEPADI en Ituri aumentaron un 200%, al pasar de 1.183 entre enero y marzo a 3.548 entre julio y septiembre.

En otra encuesta de UNICEF dirigida a unos 11.500 jóvenes de Ituri a través de U-Report, la plataforma digital de UNICEF para que los y las jóvenes compartan sus perspectivas sobre las cuestiones que les afectan, casi la mitad de las personas encuestadas afirmaron que el riesgo de sufrir violencia era mayor para las mujeres y las niñas desde que comenzó el brote. La violencia física y sexual fueron las preocupaciones más citadas.

Las mujeres y las niñas corren más riesgo de contraer la enfermedad. El cuidado de familiares enfermos, la preparación del entierro de sus seres queridos y las frecuentes visitas a centros de salud (en muchos casos, para llevar a niños y niñas enfermos) también incrementan el riesgo de infección. Todo ello se suma a una situación que ya era frágil, después de años de conflicto y desplazamientos que habían expuesto a las mujeres y las niñas a niveles alarmantes de violencia de género mucho antes de que empezara el brote. Ahora, muchas denuncian aún más violencia en sus hogares y en sus comunidades.

Desde que comenzó el brote, UNICEF y sus aliados han atendido a más de 3.300 supervivientes de violencia de género en Ituri y en Kivu del Norte y han brindado apoyo psicosocial y para la salud mental a casi 175.000 personas entre junio y octubre. Pero la protección de los niños y niñas y las mujeres, incluidos los servicios de atención a la violencia de género, sigue siendo uno de los ámbitos de respuesta con menor financiación, con un déficit del 76%.

Los resultados del seguimiento se están poniendo a disposición de los coordinadores de la respuesta al ébola para que puedan fundamentar la toma de decisiones, mientras UNICEF mantiene su llamamiento a las autoridades gubernamentales, los aliados de respuesta y los donantes para garantizar los siguientes puntos:

  • Hacer de la seguridad de las mujeres y las niñas un indicador fundamental de una respuesta eficaz al ébola. Trabajar con organizaciones locales de mujeres para detectar a tiempo los riesgos emergentes, actuar y evitar poner a las mujeres y las niñas en peligro o impedir que reciban ayuda.
  • Asegurar que los servicios destinados a las mujeres y las niñas estén disponibles, sean accesibles y reciban financiación suficiente durante todo el brote, así como establecer nuevos servicios en las zonas más afectadas por el ébola. A medida que aumentan los riesgos y crece la demanda de apoyo, es fundamental que los servicios de atención a la violencia de género –incluidos los espacios seguros– tengan capacidad para responder.
  • Incorporar el seguimiento de la violencia a la respuesta al actual brote de ébola y convertirlo en un componente de la preparación y la respuesta ante futuras emergencias de salud pública. Las organizaciones de mujeres deben formar parte oficialmente de los mecanismos de vigilancia, y deben establecerse salvaguardias que garanticen la confidencialidad y la seguridad. El seguimiento debe comenzar desde el inicio de cualquier brote.

“No hay justificación para la violencia y los abusos contra mujeres y niñas”, afirmó Russell. “Su protección debe formar parte de la respuesta al ébola, y para ello debemos tener en cuenta sus experiencias. Eso incluye priorizar la prevención y los servicios destinados a las supervivientes”, aseguró Russell.

Citas de aliados

“Desde que comenzó el brote, cada vez más mujeres y niñas acuden a nuestros espacios seguros con la esperanza de ser escuchadas y recibir apoyo y protección, sin miedo ni estigma. Los espacios seguros deben permanecer abiertos y recibir los recursos necesarios durante toda la respuesta. El seguimiento y el apoyo deberían extenderse a otras zonas de riesgo”, dijo Sandrine Lusamba, Coordinadora Nacional de SOFEPADI.

“Cuando las mujeres explican por qué la violencia ha comenzado o se ha agravado, muchas mencionan el miedo y la tensión que este brote ha llevado a sus hogares. Esas presiones pueden anticiparse. Si se mantiene el funcionamiento de los servicios existentes, se crean otros nuevos y se escucha a las mujeres a medida que se desarrolla la respuesta, se podrá evitar que esa presión se convierta en daño”, dijo la Dra. Lindsay Stark, Codirectora del Centro de Violencia y Salud de la Escuela de Salud Pública Bursky, Universidad de Washington en San Luis.

item.title: DR Congo: Gavi signe un accord avec le Serum Institute of India afin de garantir un accès rapide aux vaccins contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: GAVI Alliance

  • L’engagement d’achat anticipé de Gavi garantit l’accès jusqu’à 1,5 million de doses de ChAdOx1 BDBV, un vaccin candidat contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo développé conjointement par le Serum Institute of India et l’Oxford Vaccine Group de l’Université d’Oxford

  • Cet accord est financé par le Fonds de première riposte de Gavi, l’approvisionnement restant subordonné aux résultats des essais cliniques, ainsi qu’à l’obtention par le vaccin candidat des autorisations réglementaires nécessaires et des recommandations politiques

  • La Dre Sania Nishtar, directrice exécutive de Gavi : « Pour la deuxième urgence de santé publique de portée internationale depuis sa création, le Fonds de première riposte fonctionne comme prévu : il garantit un accès précoce et rapide aux vaccins, afin que les communautés puissent être protégées au plus vite. »

Genève, le 24 novembre 2026 – Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin a annoncé aujourd’hui avoir signé un engagement d’achat anticipé avec le Serum Institute of India (SII) et Serum Life Sciences afin de garantir l’accès jusqu’à 1,5 million de doses de ChAdOx1 BDBV, un vaccin candidat contre la souche Bundibugyo du virus Ebola. Ces doses, financées par le Fonds de première riposte* de Gavi, pourraient être achetées si les essais cliniques donnaient des résultats concluants, si les autorisations réglementaires étaient obtenues et si des recommandations politiques appropriées étaient formulées en faveur de l’utilisation du vaccin.

« Pour la deuxième urgence de santé publique de portée internationale depuis sa création, le Fonds de première riposte fonctionne comme prévu : il garantit un accès précoce et rapide aux vaccins, afin que les communautés puissent être protégées au plus vite », a déclaré la Dre Sania Nishtar, Directrice exécutive de Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin. « Alors que l’épidémie d’Ebola continue de ravager des communautés en République démocratique du Congo, nous devons agir de toute urgence pour veiller à ce que les procédures réglementaires soient en place, afin qu’il soit possible de mettre rapidement sur le marché ce vaccin candidat si les essais cliniques donnent des résultats positifs. C’est essentiel pour sauver des vies et garantir la sécurité de toutes et tous. »

À ce jour, l’épidémie actuelle d’Ebola a engendré plus de 11 600 cas et causé plus de 5 700 décès, dont la grande majorité en République démocratique du Congo. Le ChAdOx1 BDBV est l’un des deux nouveaux vaccins candidats contre le virus Ebola Bundibugyo que l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS) a recommandés pour des essais cliniques dans le cadre de l’épidémie actuelle.

Si, à l’issue des essais cliniques, le vaccin candidat obtient les autorisations réglementaires nécessaires et les recommandations du Groupe stratégique consultatif d’experts sur la vaccination de l’OMS, l’engagement d’achat anticipé de Gavi permettra de mettre rapidement ces doses à la disposition des populations touchées. Le SII a déjà produit la substance active nécessaire à la fabrication de plus d’un demi-million de doses du vaccin candidat afin d’en faciliter l’accès rapide.

Adar Poonawalla, PDG du Serum Institute of India, a déclaré : « Une riposte efficace aux épidémies exige la capacité d’agir rapidement, la préparation et la collaboration mondiale jouant un rôle essentiel pour garantir un accès rapide aux vaccins. Grâce à notre accord avec Gavi, nous franchissons une étape importante pour veiller à ce que les stocks de vaccins puissent être mobilisés sans délai. En collaborant avec l’Oxford Vaccine Group et l’Université d’Oxford pour le développement du vaccin contre Ebola, nous nous engageons à garantir aux communautés touchées l’accès aux vaccins, renforçant ainsi la réponse mondiale aux épidémies causées par la souche Bundibugyo du virus Ebola. »

L’annonce d’aujourd’hui s’inscrit dans le cadre du soutien global apporté par Gavi à la lutte contre l’épidémie actuelle d’Ebola. Jusqu’à 40 millions de dollars US provenant du mécanisme du Fonds de première riposte ont été alloués pour soutenir des accords visant à faciliter l’accès aux vaccins, tels que cet engagement d’achat anticipé. Le travail de Gavi en matière d’accès aux vaccins est mené en étroite collaboration avec la Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), ainsi qu’avec les Centres africains de contrôle et de prévention des maladies (Africa CDC), l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS), l’UNICEF et d’autres partenaires.

Une enveloppe supplémentaire de 10 millions de dollars US provenant du Fonds de première riposte – dont 6 millions de dollars US ont déjà été engagés ou décaissés à la République démocratique du Congo, à l’Ouganda, aux Centres africains de contrôle et de prévention des maladies, à l’OMS et à l’UNICEF – contribue à préserver les services de vaccination systématique dans les communautés touchées et à protéger les agentes et agents de santé en première ligne. Ervebo, un vaccin contre le virus Ebola déjà existant et autorisé pour lutter contre la souche Zaïre du virus, est également utilisé dans le cadre de protocoles de recherche clinique. Gavi a débloqué un investissement supplémentaire de 7 millions de dollars US afin de fournir 70 000 doses du vaccin Ervebo déjà disponible, provenant de la réserve mondiale financée par Gavi. Ces doses sont actuellement administrées aux populations touchées en République démocratique du Congo dans le cadre des protocoles d’usage compassionnel d’urgence de l’OMS.

Notes aux rédacteurs

* Le Fonds de première riposte existe grâce aux gouvernements qui ont investi dans cet élément déterminant de la capacité de Gavi à faire face aux épidémies et aux pandémies. Gavi tient à saluer le soutien essentiel apporté par les États-Unis, le Japon, l’Italie, l’Allemagne, la Norvège et la France, dont les engagements ont permis d’assurer le financement intégral du Fonds de première riposte de Gavi, d’un montant de 500 millions de dollars US.

Le Fonds de première riposte a également été mobilisé pour permettre une réponse rapide à l'urgence liée à la mpox en 2024. Pour en savoir plus, cliquez ici.

À propos de Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin

Gavi, l’Alliance du Vaccin est un partenariat public-privé qui aide à vacciner plus de la moitié des enfants de la planète contre certaines des maladies les plus meurtrières. L’Alliance du Vaccin rassemble les gouvernements des pays donateurs et des pays bénéficiaires, l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé, l’UNICEF, la Banque mondiale, l’industrie du vaccin, les agences techniques, la société civile, la Fondation Gates ainsi que d’autres partenaires du secteur privé. Pour consulter la liste complète des gouvernements donateurs et des autres grandes organisations qui financent le travail de Gavi, veuillez cliquer ici.

Depuis sa création en 2000, Gavi a aidé à vacciner une génération tout entière – soit plus de 1,3 milliard d'enfants – et à prévenir à terme plus de 23 millions de décès, ce qui a permis de réduire de moitié la mortalité infantile dans 78 pays à faible revenu. Gavi joue également un rôle essentiel dans l'amélioration de la sécurité sanitaire mondiale en soutenant les systèmes de santé et en finançant les stocks mondiaux de vaccins contre la maladie à virus Ebola, le choléra, la méningite, le mpox et la fièvre jaune. Après plus de deux décennies de progrès, Gavi s'attache désormais à protéger la nouvelle génération et surtout à atteindre les enfants zéro dose qui n'ont reçu aucune dose de vaccin. L'Alliance du Vaccin recourt à des mécanismes financiers innovants et aux technologies de pointe – allant de l'utilisation de drones à la biométrie – pour sauver des vies, prévenir les épidémies avant qu'elles ne se propagent et aider les pays à atteindre l'autosuffisance. item.title: Informing to protect: communities mobilized against mpox in the Republic of the Congo
item.description:
Country: Congo
Source: World Health Organization

Pointe-Noire, Republic of the Congo— Building trust is often the first step in delivering an effective public health message. In the port city of Pointe-Noire, Christelle Mgami, a community health worker in Ngoyo health district, has made this a priority in her mpox awareness activities. “To raise awareness among residents, we must first earn their trust. We need to know how to approach them, listen to their concerns and encourage them to report suspected cases," she says.

Like Mgami, 24 community health workers have been mobilized to bring prevention messages closer to communities and strengthen disease surveillance. Their work includes informing families, answering residents’ questions and encouraging people to seek care promptly if they develop suspected symptoms.

In the Republic of the Congo, mpox remains a public health concern. In 2026, 127 confirmed cases and one death were reported across six departments of the country. Pointe-Noire accounted for 113 cases, representing nearly 89% of all cases reported nationally.

The disease is transmitted through close contact with an infected person or contaminated objects. It can cause fever and skin lesions. Recognizing the signs and symptoms, understanding the modes of transmission and knowing preventive measures can help people protect themselves and limit the spread of the disease.

To support government efforts, the World Health Organization (WHO), with financial support from the Government of Japan, is working with health authorities to strengthen risk communication and community engagement. This support aims to improve the dissemination of health information, promote early detection and strengthen the reporting of alerts from communities to health services.

From 2 to 26 September 2026, WHO-supported awareness activities were conducted across the six health districts of Pointe-Noire: Lumumba, Loandjili, Tié-Tié, Mvoumvou, Ngoyo and Mongo-Mpoukou. Twenty-four community health workers engaged with households, markets, schools, places of worship, public spaces and other gathering points. Discussions focused on mpox transmission, signs and symptoms, prevention and hygiene measures and the management of cases at health facilities.

For Gabin Arsène Ambendé, a community health worker in Mvoumvou, the activities also provided an opportunity to strengthen his knowledge and better understand his role in supporting communities. “We now better understand how mpox is transmitted and how people can protect themselves. Our responsibility is to share this information in our neighbourhoods so that everyone can better protect themselves. A well-informed community is better prepared to prevent disease," he says.

A total of 74 260 people were reached across the six health districts, exceeding the initial target of 70 000 people. The activities also generated nine community alerts that were reported to the health system.

For Marie-Pierre Makykima, Risk Communication and Community Engagement Officer at the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, this mobilization must be accompanied by targeted interventions adapted to local needs. “This work enables us to review ongoing interventions, identify gaps and better direct teams to the areas most affected. It is not enough to deploy community health workers; we must ensure that their interventions genuinely contribute to disease prevention and control," she says.

The initiative is also helping to strengthen trust between communities and health services. Better-informed residents are more able to recognize the signs of disease, adopt recommended preventive measures and promptly report concerning situations.

Dr Youba Kandako, WHO Health Emergencies Officer in the Republic of Congo, emphasizes the importance of strong links between communities and health services: “It is essential that communities can quickly report suspected situations and that people are well informed about prevention measures. By working together with communities and health services, we can better protect populations and make our interventions more effective," he says.

These results highlight the importance of community-based mobilization in strengthening prevention efforts and vigilance within communities.

Behind these achievements lies the daily commitment of community health workers who inform, listen to and support people in ways that reflect their realities and needs.

In Pointe-Noire, community health workers remain key actors in efforts to prevent new transmissions and contribute to the goal of zero mpox cases.

item.title: Bangladesh: Forgotten but Not Over: Qatar Charity Keeps the Rohingya Crisis in Focus [EN/AR]
item.description:
Countries: Bangladesh, Malaysia, Myanmar, Sri Lanka
Source: Qatar Charity

Please refer to the attached files.

From food and healthcare to shelter and solar lighting, Qatar Charity continues to support Rohingya refugees across Bangladesh, Malaysia, and Sri Lanka, while expanding partnerships to keep their needs visible amid fading international attention.

Refugees’ suffering does not end when their stories disappear from global headlines. The need for food, healthcare, and safe shelter remains, no matter how prolonged their displacement or how much international attention has faded. The Rohingya crisis underscores the importance of sustained humanitarian action that goes beyond meeting immediate needs to protecting dignity and easing the burden of protracted displacement.

A report published on the website of Ghiras Magazine, a Qatar Charity publication, highlighted how Qatar Charity continues its interventions on the ground while expanding partnerships and mobilizing support. Qatar Charity has supported Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, since 2017 and expanded its assistance to Bhasan Char Island in 2021, through interventions ranging from emergency relief and essential services to improving living conditions.

Ms. Aisha Abdulrazzaq AlKuwari, Director of Humanitarian Operations at Qatar Charity, said keeping the Rohingya refugee crisis among humanitarian and funding priorities requires continued attention to their growing needs, stronger partnerships with humanitarian organizations and donors, and advocacy linked to needs data and evidence of impact on the ground to mobilize sustainable funding for life-saving interventions.

She added that Qatar Charity supports these efforts through its field presence and international partnerships, alongside initiatives and awareness campaigns that keep forgotten crises visible and encourage communities and donors to support those affected.

Support Across Three Countries

Between 2024 and 2026, Qatar Charity’s projects supporting Rohingya communities extended across Bangladesh, Malaysia, and Sri Lanka, with recorded expenditure of approximately QAR 29.5 million. The recorded beneficiary figures totaled 546,760, including 314,689 in Bangladesh, 231,840 in Malaysia, and 231 in Sri Lanka.

In Bangladesh, interventions ranged from school feeding, food baskets, and healthcare to the construction and rehabilitation of shelters, alongside cooking gas, solar lighting, and relief supplies. In Malaysia, projects focused on healthcare, food, hygiene, and personal care, while in Sri Lanka assistance included support for resident refugees and relief for new arrivals.

Six Areas of Humanitarian Response

Qatar Charity’s interventions covered six humanitarian areas. Recorded beneficiary figures included 167,330 in food and nutrition, 266,036 in health and 8,033 in shelter. A further 41,850 were recorded under non-food items, 36,525 under water and sanitation, and 26,986 under comprehensive relief. Some projects also reached host communities alongside refugees.

Among these interventions is a school feeding program for Rohingya students in Bangladesh, implemented in partnership with the World Food Programme, reaching 16,800 beneficiaries. Projects also include primary healthcare for 40,500 beneficiaries in Bangladesh, helping address essential health needs.

Partnerships to Expand the Response

International partnerships are another important part of the response. In January 2026, Qatar Charity and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) signed a Letter of Understanding (LoU) accompanied by a Data Sharing Addendum to strengthen their joint response to the humanitarian needs of Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. The cooperation focuses particularly on shelter and settlement, humanitarian relief materials, and essential services.

In June 2026, Qatar Charity also signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the International Rescue Committee (IRC) to expand support for Rohingya refugees, host communities and other vulnerable groups in Bangladesh. The partnership covers program implementation, resource mobilization, and the development of new initiatives, as well as project concepts and proposals designed to attract additional funding for life-saving assistance and resilience-building programs.

Solar Lighting: Making Everyday Life Safer and Easier

Among the more targeted interventions is a project to provide solar-powered lighting along pathways in Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, designed to reach 20,356 beneficiaries. The project responds to inadequate nighttime lighting and the difficulties this creates for movement and access to essential services.

The project is designed to install integrated solar lighting systems along pathways and in key areas of the camps. The aim is to make it easier for residents to reach health facilities, water points, and distribution centers after dark, while strengthening safety and protection and reducing dependence on electricity networks that are unavailable in many of the targeted locations.

The plan also includes training local teams in maintenance and performance monitoring, involving community members in identifying priority locations, and raising awareness of clean energy. By combining an everyday need with measures to sustain the service, the project seeks to make nighttime movement and access to essential facilities safer and easier.

item.title: Three months on from Nepal's devastating floods, thousands of children face a new threat: winter
item.description:
Country: Nepal
Source: UN Children's Fund

KATHMANDU, 25 November 2026 – Nearly three months after the devastating floods that struck Nepal on 26 August, thousands of children and families remain on a long road to recovery. While floodwaters receded, a new crisis is emerging as winter approaches, threatening children who have already lost homes, belongings, schools and access to essential services.

The floods along the Bhote Koshi River affected an estimated 84,270 people, including 32,021 children. The floods destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and washed away clothing, blankets and other essential household items, leaving thousands of children and families vulnerable to the harsh winter conditions ahead. In the hills and mountains of Nepal, winter temperatures can fall well below freezing, reaching -12°C in some areas.

"Children are still living with the consequences of the floods every day," said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. "Many have lost homes, schools, belongings and a sense of normalcy. As winter sets in, the risks facing children will only increase. No child should have to endure freezing temperatures because a disaster took away everything their family owned. Urgent support is needed now to help children stay warm, healthy, protected and learning through the winter months."

Three months after the floods, and following the initial humanitarian response, children's worries are far from over. For many children, the disaster did not end when the floodwaters receded. Trauma, psychosocial distress and protection risks remain high, while disrupted livelihoods and prolonged displacement continue to increase the risks of exploitation, violence and family separation. Mothers and newborns need access to shock-resilient, warm and well-equipped health facilities during the winter months, while approximately 30,000 children require support to continue their education through safe learning spaces, rehabilitated classrooms and learning materials. As communities move from emergency response to recovery, investing in children's protection, health and education remains critical to prevent long-term impacts on their well-being and future opportunities.

UNICEF has been on the ground since the floods occurred and has worked with the government and partners to restore access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services for more than 42,000 people, reached almost 19,500 children and their caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support, vaccinated 66,000 people against cholera, supported learning and protection of children through 52 temporary learning centres and 35 child-friendly spaces.

However, winter now presents a new set of challenges. With homes, clothing, and essential household items lost, thousands face freezing temperatures. UNICEF has already provided warm clothing to 1,472 children and distributed 1,337 thermal blankets, alongside cash assistance, heated learning spaces, and support for newborns and pregnant women. However further support is needed.

UNICEF's winterization response aims to support the most vulnerable children and families through:

  • Cash assistance for 10,000 households (approximately 50,000 people);
  • Distribution of blankets, warm clothing and winter kits for children;
  • Provision of 2,000 newborn kits containing warm clothing and essential supplies for newborns and mothers;
  • Heating systems for temporary learning spaces and health facilities;
  • Continued support for climate-resilient recovery and restoration of essential services.

"UNICEF’s winter support is not simply about keeping children warm," said Akunga. "It is about ensuring newborns survive their first months of life, helping children continue learning, protecting health and preventing families from falling deeper into crisis. Investing now will save lives and support recovery."

UNICEF’s request for supporting children and families through the winter months as well as restoring and strengthening services for children and families affected by the floods is US$47 million. Around US$30 million remains unfunded. UNICEF is calling on development partners, the private sector and the public to support urgent winterization efforts and longer-term recovery.

“As Nepal enters the coldest months of the year, the message is clear: while the floods may have passed, the emergency for children is far from over,” said Ms Akunga.

item.title: Sharp spike in landmine casualties as renewed violence intensifies in Yemen
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: HALO Trust

Aden, 25 November 2026 – Civilian deaths and injuries caused by landmines and explosive hazards in Yemen jumped five-fold in October following the resurgence of fighting and displacement, The HALO Trust warned today.

Amid the escalation of heavy fighting across the country, families are fleeing into unfamiliar and potentially contaminated territory. According to figures gathered by HALO Yemen the number of casualties surged to 98 in October, more than five times the recorded monthly average for 2026. The real number of casualties is estimated to be significantly higher.

Two particularly serious incidents alone caused 34 civilian casualties when a packed passenger bus struck an improvised explosive device (IED), while another vehicle hit a concealed landmine in the road.

“As people frantically attempt to escape the war into unknown territory, they face the additional threat of being killed or maimed by explosive devices. At the same time, Yemen’s humanitarian crisis continues to deepen as millions struggle to access the basic necessities they need to survive,” warns Phillipa Coates, HALO Yemen’s Programme Manager.

Daily life for civilians in Yemen has deteriorated rapidly as airstrikes and shifting frontlines disrupt movement and access to essential supplies.

“Severe shortages of food, clean water, fuel and essential medicines are placing an ever-greater burden on communities across the country. An estimated 2.2 million children under five are already suffering from acute malnutrition, while renewed fighting is pushing more families into increasingly desperate situations,” Coates adds.

Around 30 HALO Trust employees are among the hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped by fighting in the frontline city of Taiz, where Houthi fighters have

severed major supply and transport routes.

HALO staff report that food, diesel and fresh water are becoming increasingly scarce, with prices for basic commodities up to five times the regional average.

“The emergency in Taiz is about far more than shifting frontlines. Families are being separated, livelihoods disrupted and futures put on hold. Our colleagues are experiencing this uncertainty first-hand, cut off from their loved ones and with no clear idea when, or if, they will be able to return home.”

For interviews or further information please contact media@halotrust.org

Credit: The HALO Trust.

Notes to editors

  • The spike in landmines casualties has been recorded in Al Jawf, Taiz, Shabwah, Al Hodeidah, Al Bayda, Ad Dali’ and Hajjah governates.
  • HALO, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine clearance organisation, has worked in Yemen since 2019, starting in Aden, and beginning operations in Taiz in late 2022, with around 70 staff working across Aden, Taiz and Ad Dhale.
  • Since 2019, HALO Yemen has made more than two million square metres of land safe, destroyed over 114 tonnes of explosives, and provided explosive-ordnance safety training to more than 58,000 people.
  • HALO's Yemen programme is delivered in partnership with YEMAC.
  • HALO trains and employs Yemeni staff in specialist mine-action roles.
  • The latest UN figures available for November 2026 indicate that 22.3 million people in Yemen need humanitarian assistance, while 18.3 million are experiencing acute food insecurity. Of those facing hunger, 5.1 million are living with emergency levels of food insecurity. Children are particularly vulnerable, with an estimated 2.2 million under-fives suffering from acute malnutrition, including approximately 500,000 with severe acute malnutrition. (WFP November 2026 operational overview; WFP situation update, 2 October 2026; UN 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan).

  • Updated IPC projection analysis confirms internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Baidoa remain in IPC Acute Food Insecurity (AFI) Phase 4 (Emergency) and IPC Acute Malnutrition (AMN) Phase 4 (Critical) through December 2026.

  • Despite these improvements, acute food insecurity and malnutrition remain at emergency levels among Baidoa’s displaced population, requiring sustained humanitarian support.

item.title: World: Día internacional para la eliminación de la violencia contra la mujer
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Caritas

Con motivo del Día Internacional para la eliminación de la violencia contra la mujer, Caritas Internationalis se une a la comunidad internacional para reafirmar que esta cuestión es urgente y de justicia. El compromiso de defender la dignidad de cada persona constituye el núcleo mismo de la misión de Caritas Internationalis y es la base de todas nuestras acciones.
El papa León XIV reafirmó recientemente (véase el Viaje apostólico a Perú, Discurso en la plaza frente a la catedral de Lima) que «el reconocimiento de la dignidad humana exige que promovamos eficazmente la presencia, el respeto y la participación de las mujeres», y ha destacado lo tristeágico que es que «la violencia contra las mujeres (…) siga siendo una realidad que hiere a toda la humanidad», lanzando un ardiente llamamiento «a todos los hombres y mujeres de buena voluntad: ¡valoremos a las mujeres! ¡protejamos y respetemos a las niñas!» (cf. Magnifica humanitas, 57).
Caritas se hace eco con fuerza de este llamamiento, convencida de que abordar esta cuestión es una prioridad urgente y absoluta que exige una responsabilidad compartida a todos los niveles, desde el local hasta el global. Este compromiso está en el centro de nuestro trabajo diario: acompañar a las comunidades, caminar junto a las mujeres y las niñas.
Según las Naciones Unidas, «la violencia contra la mujer sigue siendo una de las violaciones de los derechos humanos más generalizadas en todo el mundo, que afecta a una de cada tres mujeres a lo largo de su vida»: una situación que hay que abordar mediante el refuerzo de los mecanismos seguros de denuncia, el acceso a servicios centrados en las supervivientes, la aplicación efectiva de las leyes y una mayor rendición de cuentas por parte de los autores y las instituciones. El lema de este año, «Garantizar la justicia, proteger a las supervivientes, acabar con la impunidad», nos invita a reflexionar sobre los sistemas jurídicos, pero también sobre las vías que se ofrecen a las mujeres y niñas que sufren violencia.
Caritas se compromete a proporcionar espacios seguros para la mujer en todo el mundo, ofreciendo servicios clave como asesoramiento, apoyo psicológico, formación profesional y programas de oportunidades laborales. Este compromiso se extiende también a la prevención de la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas y a la lucha contra sus causas estructurales, a través de iniciativas para promover la igualdad, el empoderamiento y un cambio duradero hacia una sociedad más justa e inclusiva. En todos los continentes, incluidas las zonas de conflicto, Caritas trabaja desde las comunidades de base para garantizar que la mujer disfrute de poder y capacidad de acción en su comunidad y en la sociedad en general. Tiene que ser escuchada, protegida, bienvenida y acompañada. Es necesario crear soluciones adaptadas a sus necesidades y a los contextos en los que vive, de acuerdo con las normas internacionales. Caritas observa y reconoce que la violencia contra la mujer se comete de forma generalizada en todas partes, que siempre constituye una tragedia personal, y valora la labor de su personal y sus voluntarios, que llegan incluso a las zonas más remotas del mundo para prestar apoyo a través de una amplia gama de acciones, con profesionalidad y humanidad.
«Caritas se compromete a trabajar con las mujeres y las niñas víctimas de violencia para que se sientan más seguras, cada día en nuestro trabajo, en las comunidades de base. Hay que ofrecerles semillas tangibles de esperanza para su futuro. Al mismo tiempo, como Caritas, renovamos nuestro compromiso institucional de reforzar nuestros sistemas de salvaguardia y de proteger a las mujeres, las niñas y cualquier persona vulnerable, frente a toda forma de violencia, explotación, abuso, acoso o discriminación. Para nosotros, se trata de un imperativo legal, una obligación moral y una llamada del Evangelio”, afirma Alistair Dutton, secretario general de Caritas Internationalis.
﻿

Countries: Afghanistan, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, France, Germany, Italy, Montenegro, Northern Mariana Islands (The United States of America), Serbia
Source: International Organization for Migration

Ginebra, 25 de noviembre de 2026 – Los nacionales afganos que transitan por la ruta de los Balcanes Occidentales describen trayectos que duran meses y cuestan miles de euros, según nuevos datos de la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM). Aunque ha disminuido el número de nacionales afganos registrados en las principales rutas hacia Europa, quienes aún emprenden el viaje describen desplazamientos marcados por dificultades económicas e incertidumbre.

Entre enero y agosto de 2026, las autoridades de los Balcanes Occidentales registraron a 3.941 nacionales afganos, lo que representa el 17 % de las personas registradas en esta ruta. Los nacionales afganos han sido sistemáticamente uno de los grupos más numerosos registrados en ella, con un promedio anual del 21 % de los registros desde 2020.

"Con demasiada frecuencia, la migración se analiza desde una única perspectiva», afirmó Mihyung Park, Jefa de Misión de la OIM en Afganistán. «La movilidad afgana hoy en día es compleja y se produce en múltiples direcciones. Mientras muchas familias reconstruyen sus vidas en Afganistán, otras permanecen en países vecinos o continúan sus viajes, impulsadas por presiones económicas, los efectos del clima y la incertidumbre".

La OIM entrevistó a 1.045 nacionales afganos que transitaban por la ruta de los Balcanes Occidentales a través de Albania, Bosnia y Herzegovina, Montenegro, Macedonia del Norte, Serbia y Kosovo¹. La mediana de la duración del viaje entre las personas encuestadas fue de 209 días, lo que significa que la mitad de ellas llevaba viajando más tiempo. Las personas encuestadas gastaron una media de 7.541 euros, el costo más elevado entre los diez grupos de nacionalidad más numerosos encuestados. Más de una de cada cinco gastó más de 10.000 euros, mientras que el 37 % aún tenía deudas relacionadas con su viaje.

Las personas encuestadas citaron diversos factores que influyeron en sus decisiones de abandonar Afganistán. Si bien las motivaciones variaron entre quienes fueron encuestados a lo largo de la ruta de los Balcanes Occidentales, los informes recientes de seguimiento de la OIM en Afganistán han destacado sistemáticamente la importancia de las presiones económicas, los medios de subsistencia y las oportunidades de empleo en las decisiones relacionadas con la movilidad.

La gran mayoría de las personas encuestadas manifestó su intención de continuar el viaje. Todas tenían previsto seguir viajando hacia otros países europeos, siendo Italia (37 %), Alemania (22 %) y Francia (20 %) los destinos previstos más frecuentemente mencionados. Los vínculos familiares influyeron considerablemente en la elección de estos destinos. Más de dos tercios declararon que no tenían intención de regresar a Afganistán.

Los resultados se producen en un contexto de dinámicas migratorias más amplias que afectan a Afganistán, incluido el retorno de 1,4 millones de afganos desde la República Islámica del Irán y Pakistán en lo que va de 2026, lo que ejerce una presión adicional sobre comunidades que ya enfrentan dificultades económicas y necesidades relacionadas con el invierno.

A medida que los gobiernos y los socios humanitarios responden a los cambios en las dinámicas migratorias, contar con datos fiables sigue siendo fundamental para comprender quiénes se desplazan, por qué lo hacen y qué tipo de apoyo pueden necesitar a lo largo del camino. El informe contribuye a fortalecer la base empírica para la formulación de políticas e intervenciones en los países de origen, tránsito y destino.

Nota para los editores

Las autoridades de los Balcanes Occidentales registraron a 3.941 nacionales afganos entre enero y agosto de 2026.

La OIM entrevistó a 1.045 nacionales afganos en 22 ubicaciones de seis territorios de los Balcanes Occidentales.

Los resultados se refieren únicamente a las personas encuestadas y no deben interpretarse como representativos de todos los nacionales afganos que viajan hacia Europa.

El informe completo está disponible aquí: Europa — Nacionales afganos que viajan hacia y a través de los Balcanes Occidentales en 2026.

Para más información, visite el Centro de Medios de Comunicación de la OIM.

1Las referencias a Kosovo deben entenderse en el contexto de la resolución 1244 (1999) del Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas.

item.title: Technical workshop in Syria advances disaster risk knowledge for inclusive multi-hazard early warning systems and anticipatory action
item.description:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

Understanding who is at risk, where vulnerabilities lie and how hazards interact is fundamental to developing effective early warning systems. In Syria, this requires particular attention to population displacement, disrupted infrastructure and the availability of reliable risk information.

From 16 to 18 November 2026, the technical workshop on Advancing Risk Knowledge for Inclusive Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems in Syria brought together national institutions, technical experts, and humanitarian and development partners to establish a common, nationally owned technical foundation for strengthening disaster risk knowledge.

The workshop connected Pillar 1 of the Early Warnings for All (EW4All) initiative with the European Union-funded project on Enhancing Emergency Preparedness and Response in Syria (EEPR) through multi-hazard early warning systems and anticipatory action protocols.

The project brings together the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), Mercy Corps, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), and the Danish Refugee Council (DRC).

Building a common understanding of risk

A central focus of the workshop was examining how existing risk assessments, datasets, monitoring systems and institutional expertise could inform a more comprehensive understanding of Syria's risk landscape.

UNDRR provided technical guidance on integrating hazard, exposure, vulnerability and impact information within the EW4All framework, while FAO contributed its expertise in climate risk assessment.

Technical sessions examined the availability, quality, accessibility, and geographical coverage of existing data, alongside institutional responsibilities for collecting, managing, and sharing risk information.

An important component was the development of a common approach to hazard and risk profiling. This included examining historical impacts, hazard frequency and severity, populations at risk, monitoring indicators, and interactions between different hazards.

The process is intended to inform the development of ten hazard profiles under the EEPR project , providing an evidence base for early warning systems, anticipatory action protocols, and disaster risk reduction planning.

Who could still be left behind?

An early warning system cannot fulfil its purpose if the people most at risk are absent from the data or unable to access the information it provides.

Through the application of UNDRR's Inclusive Early Warning and Early Action Checklist, the workshop examined how gender, age, disability, displacement, language, and geographical location can influence access to risk information and warnings.

Discussions also explored the integration of population mobility projections into risk assessments, recognizing the importance of understanding changing patterns of exposure to improve impact forecasting and anticipatory decision-making.

Beyond accessibility, participants examined the operational challenges of maintaining early warning services in fragile and conflict-affected settings. These included infrastructure damage, communication disruptions, institutional constraints, and the protection and security considerations associated with collecting and sharing sensitive information.

The emphasis was on designing systems that reflect people's circumstances and remain functional when they are needed most.

From technical assessments to national priorities

The workshop's roadmap discussions centred on translating identified gaps into practical actions, supported by clear institutional responsibilities, partnerships, and resource requirements.

Working-group exercises provided a framework for connecting each identified gap with the evidence supporting it, the capabilities required to address it and the proposed interventions. This approach is intended to inform immediate, medium- and longer-term priorities under Syria's EW4All roadmap.

By bringing the EW4All process and the EEPR project together, the workshop represents a step towards aligning existing expertise, investments, and institutional capacities under national leadership.

Ultimately, strengthening disaster risk knowledge in Syria is about ensuring that the information available to institutions and communities can guide decisions before emergencies unfold, helping protect lives and livelihoods through timely, inclusive, and informed action.

item.title: Algeria: Strengthening disaster preparedness and inclusive crisis response across North Africa through regional cooperation and risk knowledge
item.description:
Countries: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia
Source: UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction

Across North Africa, disasters are becoming increasingly complex, with climate-related hazards, displacement and population movements placing growing pressure on national preparedness and response systems. Strengthening resilience requires more than responding to emergencies as they unfold. It begins with understanding risks, anticipating their consequences and ensuring that preparedness measures account for the needs of all communities.

Against this backdrop, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), through its Regional Office for Arab States (ROAS), contributed to the regional workshop Strengthening Preparedness in North Africa , held in Cairo from 10 to 12 November 2026.

Organized by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) under the European Union-funded Regional Development and Protection Programme for North Africa (RDPP-NA), the three-day workshop brought together representatives from Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco and Tunisia to strengthen national preparedness capacities, foster regional cooperation and promote more inclusive approaches to crisis management.

Strengthening preparedness through disaster risk knowledge

A central contribution from UNDRR ROAS focused on the role of disaster data and statistics in strengthening tsunami emergency preparedness.

During a technical session, Raidan Al Saqqaf, Deputy Chief of UNDRR ROAS, addressed how disaster data can inform preparedness planning and support risk-informed decision-making.

The session reinforced the importance of understanding hazards, exposure, and vulnerabilities before emergencies occur. Reliable disaster data provides a foundation for identifying risks, informing contingency planning, and strengthening the capacity of national institutions to anticipate and prepare for potential impacts.

By bringing a disaster risk reduction perspective into discussions on crisis management and human mobility, UNDRR highlighted the importance of connecting risk knowledge with coordinated preparedness measures, particularly in contexts where disasters may trigger displacement or compound existing vulnerabilities.

Putting preparedness to the test

Building on the technical exchanges, the workshop featured a scenario-based tabletop exercise designed to examine the challenges of managing emergencies involving displacement and cross-border population movements.

Participants worked through simulated crisis situations involving flooding, population displacement, and emerging protection needs. Through stakeholder interactions and coordination exercises, they explored how national institutions can exchange information, identify response priorities, and address the needs of migrants and other vulnerable groups during emergencies.

The exercise provided an opportunity to consider how disaster preparedness systems can better account for the human dimensions of crises, particularly where overlapping risks place additional pressure on national and local response capacities.

Translating regional learning into national action

The workshop concluded with country-level discussions focused on identifying preparedness gaps and practical measures to improve coordination and migrant inclusion in disaster preparedness, response, and recovery.

Participants reviewed national arrangements and examined how lessons from the simulation could inform preparedness checklists and country-specific priorities.

These exchanges highlighted the value of regional cooperation in addressing shared risks while recognizing the different institutional arrangements and preparedness needs of participating countries.

Advancing inclusive and risk-informed resilience

For UNDRR ROAS, the workshop provided an opportunity to reinforce the importance of integrating disaster risk knowledge into broader crisis preparedness efforts.

As climate-related hazards and human mobility increasingly intersect across North Africa, strengthening national capacities to understand and anticipate risks remains essential to protecting lives, livelihoods, and communities.

The discussions underscored a shared priority: preparedness must be informed by evidence, supported by effective coordination and inclusive of those most vulnerable to disasters.

Through its technical contribution and engagement with regional partners, UNDRR ROAS continues to promote risk-informed approaches that support stronger national preparedness systems and advance disaster resilience across the Arab region.
